Home/Yard/Mowing-the-lawn.title: Mowing the lawn
Home/Yard/Mowing-the-lawn.content:
Kentucky bluegrass will grow about 1-2 inches (25-51 mm) per week in its peak season. I plan to cut to a height of 42 mm, and you want to cut one-third or less of the grass in one mowing, so at least once a week is best in the growing season. The best grass height from when I should mow it is 63 mm (2½”). My handbreadth is about 80 mm.

Recipes/Corn-on-the-cob.title: Corn on the cob
Recipes/Corn-on-the-cob.content:
Ingredients

Fresh ears of corn
1 tbsp lemon juice (optional)
Salt (optional)
Butter (optional)

Instructions

Fill a large pot with enough water to fully submerge the corn cobs
Optionally add a pinch of salt and/or lemon juice
Bring the water to a rolling boil over high heat
Shuck the corn. Leaving the husk on gives it more of a steamed flavor and texture, and removing the husk makes it crisper
Cover and boil for 7 minutes
Check the corn for doneness by inserting a knife or fork into a kernel. If it easily pierces through, it’s ready.
Optional brush with melted butter

Recipes/Corned-beef.title: Corned beef
Recipes/Corned-beef.content:
Ingredients
Brining:

400 ml water
2 tbsp salt
1 tbsp brown sugar
¼ tsp pink curing salt
2 tsp pickling spices
1 kg beef brisket

Cooking:

1¾ cups water or beef broth
1½ tsp pickling spices
1 large carrot peeled and cut into 2” pieces
½ lb small red potatoes cut in half
½ head green cabbage core removed and quartered

Instructions
Brining:

In a Dutch oven or large stock pot add the water, kosher salt, brown sugar, pickling spices, pink curing salt, garlic and stir. Bring to a boil, lower to simmer and cook until salt and sugar have dissolved. Turn off heat and cool.
In a large sealable plastic bag place beef brisket. Pour cooled brine over and cover or seal. Store in a refrigerator for 5 days, turning beef on day 3. On day 5 remove from brine liquid and follow the directions to cook. Discard brine.

Cooking:

Add beef, water or beef broth, and pickling spices and cook on low for about 7-8 hours. Add carrot and potatoes at the half time mark and add the cabbage in the last 2 hours.
Remove corned beef and cover with foil to keep warm at least 15-20 minutes.
When ready to serve, slice the brisket against the grain in ¼” or thinner slices. If you cut with the grain it will be stringy.

Notes

I’ve adapted the original recipe to use a plastic bag and therefore about ¼ as much brine. Regardless of brining method, the brine should be made with the same ratios otherwise the meat will be too strongly flavored.
I’ve also adapted the original recipe to be based on 1 kg of brisket

Recipes/Pickling-spices.title: Pickling spices
Recipes/Pickling-spices.content:
Ingredients

1 tbsp yellow mustard seeds
1 tbsp black mustard seeds
1 tbsp whole allspice (or 1 tsp ground)
1 tbsp juniper berries (or excluded altogether?)
2 tsp coriander seeds (or ½ tsp ground)
2 tsp black peppercorns
2 tsp dill seeds (or 1 tsp carraway seed and optionally 1 tsp celery seed?)
1 tsp red pepper flakes
1 tsp ground ginger
8 whole cloves
5 green cardamom pods
3 bay leaves
2 star anise
1 3-inch cinnamon stick

Instructions

Mix together the first 9 ingredients in a small bowl.
In a spice grinder add the cloves, cardamom pods, bay leaves, star anise and cinnamon stick. Pulse several times, but do not make it a complete powder. Keep it in small pieces. Add to spices in bowl and mix to combine.
Store in an air tight container for your pickling recipes. Makes about a 1/2 cup.

Tips

You can use all yellow or all black mustard seeds if one or the other is not available.

Recipes/Play-dough.title: Play dough
Recipes/Play-dough.content:
From: Cathy Culberson
Ingredients

2 cups flour
1 cup salt
2 tbsp. oil
4 tsp. cream of tartar
2 cups water

Instructions

Mix all ingredients
Cook at medium heat until thick, stirring constantly. Ball will form.
Remove from heat. Put on waxed paper. Knead several times.
Add food coloring

Recipes/Poached-eggs.title: Poached eggs
Recipes/Poached-eggs.content:
Ingredients

Up to 4 eggs

Instructions

Heat 1½ inches (4 cm) of water in a skillet to 190°F (88°C), enough that some bubbles form on the bottom but not enough that it’s boiling. You should be able to stick your finger in the water briefly and pull it out.
Break eggs into ramekins or small bowls
Gently lower the ramekins or bowls into the water and tip the eggs into it, ensuring you don’t break the yolk
Poach for 4 minutes and 30 seconds
Remove the eggs with a slotted spoon onto a towel. You can cut away the edges so it looks smoother.

Recipes/Pulled-pork.title: Pulled pork
Recipes/Pulled-pork.content:
Ingredients

1 (5 pound) bone-in pork shoulder roast
1 tbsp salt
ground black pepper
1½ cups (350 ml) apple cider vinegar
2 tablespoons brown sugar
1½ tablespoons hot pepper sauce
2 teaspoons cayenne pepper
2 teaspoons crushed red pepper flakes

Instructions

Place the pork shoulder into a slow cooker and season with salt and pepper. Pour the vinegar around the pork. Cover, and cook on Low for 12 hours. Pork should easily pull apart into strands.
Remove the pork from the slow cooker and discard any bones. Strain out the liquid, and save 2 cups. Discard any extra. Shred the pork using tongs or two forks, and return to the slow cooker. Stir the brown sugar, hot pepper sauce, cayenne pepper, and red pepper flakes into the reserved sauce. Mix into the pork in the slow cooker. Cover and keep on Low setting until serving.

Recipes/Steak.title: Steak
Recipes/Steak.content:
Ingredients

1 boneless beef steak, up to 1 inch thick (about 2 pounds total), such as strip, rib-eye, flat iron, chuck-eye, hanger or skirt (preferably “outside” skirt)
Coarse salt
Black pepper

Instructions

Thaw steaks outside the fridge. Don’t use water unless you’re very confident about a vacuum-packed steak.
Remove packaging and pat meat dry with paper towels. Line a plate with paper towels, place meat on top and set aside to dry further and come to cool room temperature (30 to 60 minutes, depending on the weather). Turn occasionally; replace paper towels as needed.
Heat cast iron skillet in oven at 500°F (260°C)
Remove cast iron skillet from oven and place on range. Turn heat to high under pan. Pat both sides of steak dry again.
When pan is smoking hot, 5 to 8 minutes, pat steak dry again, sprinkle with copious amounts of salt and pepper, and place in pan. (If using two steaks, cook in two batches.)
Let steak sizzle for 1 minute, then use tongs to flip it over, moving raw side of steak around in pan so both sides are salted. Press down gently to ensure even contact between steak and pan. Keep cooking over very high heat, flipping steak after another 1 minute.
Move steak to oven and let cook for 2 minutes, then flip and let cook for another 2 minutes. Reduce time for thinner steaks.
When steak has contracted in size and developed a dark-brown crust, check for doneness. To the touch, meat should feel softly springy but not squishy. If using an instant-read thermometer, insert into side of steak. For medium-rare meat, 120 to 125 degrees is ideal: Steak will continue cooking after being removed from heat.
If making a pan sauce, mix in a bit of butter and optional red wine, spooning on top of steak until butter stops foaming
Remove steak to an upside-down plate on cutting board and tent lightly with foil. The plate ensures the juices drip away from meat instead of pooling underneath it and making the crust soggy. Let rest 5 minutes.
Serve in pieces or thickly slice on the diagonal, cutting away from your body and with the top edge of the knife leaning toward your body. If cooking skirt or hanger steak, make sure to slice across the grain of the meat. Drizzle any pan sauce you’ve made on top of the steak.

Recipes/Vanilla-bean-paste.title: Vanilla bean paste
Recipes/Vanilla-bean-paste.content:
Ingredients

30 vanilla beans
6 tbsp vanilla extract
1⅔ cups maple syrup (or agave syrup)

Instructions

Place all the ingredients in a food processor and puree until smooth (you can chop up the vanilla beans if you want to save some time).
Place a fine mesh strainer over a bowl and pour the mixture inside.
Press on the vanilla bean pulp to get as much liquid out as possible. Pour the strained vanilla paste liquid into a jar and seal tightly. You can reuse the pulp to steep in homemade vanilla extract.  Store the vanilla paste in the fridge.

Recipes/Vanilla-extract.title: Vanilla extract
Recipes/Vanilla-extract.content:
Ingredients

5-6 vanilla beans
1 cup vodka, rum or bourbon
One 8+ oz bottle or jar with a tight seal

Instructions

Using a sharp knife, slit the vanilla beans so the beans are exposed. No need to completely split the bean in half, just slit down the middle. If the length of the vanilla beans don’t fit into your bottle or jar, cut the vanilla beans into smaller pieces. Place beans into bottle or jar.
Pour vodka on top. A funnel helps. Use a little extra vodka, if needed, so the beans are fully submerged. Shake a few times.
Store vanilla at room temperature out of direct sunlight. Shake about once per week or once every couple weeks. Vanilla can be ready to use in as little as 8 weeks, but I recommend at least 6 months for optimal flavor. 12+ months is great!
As you begin to use your vanilla, you can refill with a little vodka each time. Give it a shake after you refill and give it a shake before each use, too. If you’re gifting the vanilla or if you don’t have any more alcohol to refill, remove the beans completely after first use. The beans will become a little slimy if they aren’t almost fully submerged.
Unused aged vanilla extract (with the beans fully submerged) will last several years. If it still smells good, it’s still good to use! Aged extract without the beans will last indefinitely. Once you begin using the vanilla and adding more alcohol after each use, the beans will eventually need to be replaced. It’s hard to give a specific amount of time as some may use (and refill) the vanilla more quickly than others. After about 1 year of frequent use and refilling, you will you find the vanilla flavor less intense. Simply remove old beans, add fresh beans, shake, and continue to use/refill.

Tips
Single fold vanilla extract uses 4 beans per cup of alcohol, and this is what most store-bought brands do. Double fold is 8 beans. This recipe is in between to balance taste and cost-effectiveness.
For choosing an alcohol:

Vodka - Pure vanilla bean taste
Bourbon - Enhanced vanilla bean taste with smokey and sweet notes
Rum - Maximum vanilla taste, aroma and sweetness

For choosing a vanilla bean origin:

Madagascar - Very common and has a creamy and rich flavor
Tahiti - Very common and has a rich almost floral flavor
Mexico - Darker almost smoky flavor

Recipes/Œufs-cocotte.title: Œufs cocotte
Recipes/Œufs-cocotte.content:
Ingredients

Butter or olive oil
Eggs

Instructions

Pour water into a saucepan such that it’s half the height of the ramekins. Bring to a low boil.
Butter any ramekins
Place any spices, meats or cheeses in the ramekins
Add an egg to each ramekin, taking care not to break the yolk
Optionally, cover with crème fraîche, season with salt and pepper, and sprinkle with Gruyère to finish
Simmer for 7 minutes
Pour out any water that’s accumulated in the ramekins

You can also bake these in a hot water bath in the oven, but that’s more work

Zero-GC-Java.title: Zero GC Java
Zero-GC-Java.content:
These are just a few notes on how to write Java without garbage collection or runtime memory allocation. While it might seem absurd to use a garbage collected language when we don’t want garbage collection, that’s what we do today.
First, you need Object pools
